title: Field study of office worker responses to fluorescent lighting of different CCT and lumen output
research_question: To examine the effects of correlated color temperature (CCT) and lumen output of fluorescent lighting on office occupants' visual comfort, brightness perception, satisfaction, and self-reported productivity.

participants.description: Mean age = 38.8 years (range 23-55 years), 11 male, 15 female, 24 White, 2 Black/African American. Office workers in Central Pennsylvania. 10 participants had daylight access in their personal work areas, 16 did not.
participants.recruitment: All individuals working in the space were approached via e-mail, telephone, or in person to participate.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four luminous conditions created by commercially available linear fluorescent lamps (T8, CRI 82-85) in a 2x2 factorial design: (1) 3500 K, 2330 lm (Lamp A); (2) 5000 K, ~3000 lm (Lamp B); (3) 3500 K, ~3000 lm (Lamp C); (4) 5000 K, 2330 lm (Lamp D). Each condition lasted two weeks, with the first week for adaptation.

measures.instrument: EMA1: 'how satisfied were you with the visual comfort of the electric lighting in your work area?' (0-100 scale, 0=very unsatisfactory, 100=very satisfactory)
EMA2: 'how bright was the lighting in your work area?' (0-100 scale, 0=too dim, 100=too bright)

Web2: 'Overall, I am satisfied with the lighted environment of my work area.' (7-point Likert scale)
Web3: 'Overall, I am satisfied with the electric lighting in my work area.' (7-point Likert scale)
Web4: 'The lighting in my work area is pleasant to work under.' (7-point Likert scale)

measures.construct: Light quantity for reading printed materials
measures.instrument: Web5: 'There is enough light to read printed materials at my desk.' (7-point Likert scale)

Web7: 'The quantity of electric lighting for the work that I do is:' (1=too dim, 5=too bright)

Web14: 'The light is appropriately distributed for my visual tasks.' (7-point Likert scale)

mechanisms: The study implicitly tests the 'spectrally enhanced lighting' (SEL) method, which posits that higher CCT lamps with lower lumen output can maintain equivalent brightness perception and visual acuity. The findings suggest that while brightness perception might be maintained, other factors like visual comfort, satisfaction, and productivity are compromised.

The perception of 'cool' vs 'warm' color temperature influences comfort and satisfaction, potentially due to ecological associations with daylight and time of day (e.g., cooler light being perceived as less comfortable indoors, especially when daylight is also present).
moderators: Daylight access (presence or absence of a window in the personal work area)
implementation_implications: The U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) advocacy for 'spectrally enhanced lighting' (SEL) as an energy-saving strategy is not supported by this study, as higher CCT, even if perceived as brighter, compromises occupant comfort, satisfaction, and productivity.

Designers should consider the negative impact of higher CCT lighting (e.g., 5000K) on visual comfort, overall satisfaction, and self-reported productivity, especially in office environments and for occupants with access to daylight.
The perceived color temperature of lighting is a critical factor for occupant satisfaction, with warmer CCTs (e.g., 3500K) generally preferred over cooler ones (e.g., 5000K) in office settings.

limitations: The study was a field study, making it impractical to counterbalance the order of the four lamp types, which could introduce potential order bias (though tested and found not significant for most questions).
The sample size (N=26) is relatively small, which might limit generalizability.
The study focused on within-subject differences, and while an order effect was tested, it might not fully capture all potential biases from the fixed sequence of conditions.
The study did not directly measure visual acuity, which is a key claim of the SEL method.
The study did not directly measure physiological responses (e.g., cortisol, melatonin) to lighting conditions.
The study did not include a full range of CCTs or lumen outputs, limiting the scope of generalization.

paper_metadata.title: Individual differences in mental imagery in different modalities and levels of intentionality
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Individual differences in mental imagery in different modalities and levels of intentionality
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Mental imagery is a highly common component of everyday cognitive functioning. While substantial progress is being made in clarifying this fundamental human function, much is still unclear or unknown. A more comprehensive account of mental imagery aspects would be gained by examining individual differences in age, sex, and background experience in an activity and their association with imagery in different modalities and intentionality levels. The current online study combined multiple imagery self-report measures in a sample (
                    n
                    = 279) with a substantial age range (18–65 years), aiming to identify whether age, sex, or background experience in sports, music, or video games were associated with aspects of imagery in the visual, auditory, or motor stimulus modality and voluntary or involuntary intentionality level. The findings show weak positive associations between age and increased vividness of voluntary auditory imagery and decreased involuntary musical imagery frequency, weak associations between being female and more vivid visual imagery, and relations of greater music and video game experience with higher involuntary musical imagery frequency. Moreover, all imagery stimulus modalities were associated with each other, for both intentionality levels, except involuntary musical imagery frequency, which was only related to higher voluntary auditory imagery vividness. These results replicate previous research but also contribute new insights, showing that individual differences in age, sex, and background experience are associated with various aspects of imagery such as modality, intentionality, vividness, and frequency. The study’s findings can inform the growing domain of applications of mental imagery to clinical and pedagogical settings.
